name: Marc Andreessen
description: Open with one declaration, then build the case in short repeated blocks. Total conviction, builder's optimism.
scope: His essays Why Software Is Eating the World (2011), It's Time to Build (2020), Why AI Will Save the World (2023) and The Techno-Optimist Manifesto (2023) on a16z.com, and his X posts from 2026. It studies manifesto, argument and recommendation writing, not his political posts, podcasts or investment memos.
strengths: Writing a bold mission statement or manifesto
limitations: The combative certainty can alienate readers when the subject is not a fight.
Long repeated blocks need real substance in each line or they read as slogans.

sources.title: It's Time to Build
sources.note: Opens by declaring that every institution failed, refuses to blame one side, lists concretely what we do not have with exclamation fragments, and turns the list into a call to build with the key verb in italics.

sources.title: Why AI Will Save the World
sources.note: A colloquial opening line, a plain definition, then numbered risks phrased as questions in headings, each answered with history or an economic framework.

sources.title: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
sources.note: One-line paragraphs in long runs that begin with the same words, first listing what we are told, then what we believe, separated by one-word headings.

sources.title: It turns out DIGGER is a work of pure cinematic genius
sources.note: A recommendation with the title in capitals, a superlative verdict, a star rating and an instruction to go without reading anything about it.

sources.title: 2026 is the best year for film since 2015
sources.note: A trend declared with examples in capitals, a comparison to a past peak with its own examples in brackets, and a short closing verdict.

sources.title: Why Software Is Eating the World
sources.note: The essay that named software taking over old industries; the source of the phrase.

observations.trait: Essays open with one declarative sentence that frames the whole argument.
Force comes from repetition: long runs of short paragraphs beginning with the same words.
Arguments are organised as numbered questions answered plainly, with concrete lists as evidence.
Recommendations are verdicts in capitals with ratings and an instruction to go.
One framing sentence before the argument: "Every Western institution was unprepared for the coronavirus pandemic, despite many prior warnings."
A run of sentences with the same opening: "We had a problem of darkness, so we invented electric lighting."
The received view, stated flatly to be overturned: "We are told to be angry, bitter, and resentful about technology."
What should exist, stacked as questions: "Where are the millions of delivery drones?"
The real problem named in a few words: "The problem is desire."
A worry raised as a numbered question: "AI Risk #1: Will AI Kill Us All?"
A verdict with the title in capitals: "It turns out DIGGER is a work of pure cinematic genius"

illustration.brief: After eight months of building, we launch our app on Friday. It turns voice notes into a to-do list. Free for the first month.
illustration.text:
After eight months of building, we launch on Friday.

The app does one thing: you talk, and it turns your voice notes into a to-do list.

This is what technology is for. Less friction. More doing.

First month is free. Just go try it.
